summary: This document specifies how SCTP can run on top of DTLS. SCTP itself does not know about the encryption, so the combination protects SCTP packets and can pass through places where plain SCTP would not work. It is used for WebRTC data channels.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8261 defines how SCTP packets travel as data inside DTLS. SCTP gains DTLS protection, but it cannot use multiple network addresses for one association.

questions: how to run sctp over dtls

subtitle: How to carry complete SCTP packets inside DTLS records.

tldr.problem: SCTP normally runs over IPv4 or IPv6, but some applications need it to use a secure datagram layer such as DTLS.
tldr.mechanism: The sender gives each complete SCTP packet to DTLS as application data. The receiver passes the decrypted DTLS payload to SCTP.
tldr.outcome: This encapsulation can provide confidentiality, source authentication, integrity and a NAT traversal path. SCTP associations carried this way are single-homed because SCTP cannot see lower-layer addresses.

today: RFC 8261 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2017. It has been updated by RFC 8899 and RFC 8996.

sections.title: Where SCTP over DTLS Fits
sections.content:
Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) normally runs over IPv4 or IPv6. RFC 8261 places Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) below SCTP, with ICE/UDP beneath DTLS in the stack shown by the RFC. The WebRTC protocol suite is given as an example use for carrying non-SRTP data between browsers.

The combination can provide confidentiality, source authentication and integrity protection, and it can help with NAT traversal. SCTP does not know which protocols operate below DTLS, so SCTP's address-management procedures do not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS carries SCTP packets as data, while SCTP continues to handle its own transport functions. SCTP cannot use information about the network addresses hidden below DTLS.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
When SCTP provides a packet to DTLS, the entire packet becomes the payload of the DTLS application-layer protocol. That packet includes the SCTP common header and its chunks.

When DTLS processes a record containing an application-layer message, it passes the payload to SCTP. SCTP then reads its common header and chunks as usual. The encapsulation does not define another SCTP packet format.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender places the whole SCTP packet inside a DTLS message. At the other end, DTLS passes the recovered packet back to SCTP.

sections.title: Path MTU and DTLS Requirements
sections.content:
An implementation MUST use a path maximum transmission unit (MTU) discovery method that works without ICMP. Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery is RECOMMENDED. DTLS MUST support version 1.0 and SHOULD support the most recently published DTLS version; DTLS 1.2 was the newest version when this RFC appeared.

SCTP performs segmentation and reassembly, so DTLS MUST NOT compress data and MUST support messages larger than the current path MTU, even if IP fragmentation results. If SCTP performs IPv4 path MTU discovery, DTLS SHOULD let it set the Don't Fragment bit. If that is unavailable, the RFC RECOMMENDS a safe MTU no greater than 1200 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP controls packet sizing, so DTLS must not compress its data. The two layers need a way to discover a safe packet size without depending on ICMP.

sections.title: Restrictions on SCTP Associations
sections.content:
A DTLS connection MUST exist before an SCTP association is established. Multiple SCTP associations MAY share one DTLS connection; SCTP port numbers separate them. Each association MUST be single-homed because DTLS exposes no address management to SCTP.

INIT and INIT-ACK chunks MUST NOT contain IPv4 or IPv6 address parameters, and INIT MUST NOT contain the Supported Address Types parameter. The implementation MUST NOT depend on processing ICMP or ICMPv6 packets. If a lower layer reports a path change, SCTP SHOULD retest the MTU and reset its congestion state.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS hides network addresses from SCTP. As a result, SCTP associations use one path and must leave address parameters out of their setup messages.

sections.title: SCTP Extensions and Security
sections.content:
The padding extension MUST be supported and used for SCTP path-MTU probes when SCTP performs discovery. If dynamic address reconfiguration is used, ASCONF chunks MUST use wildcard addresses only. The RFC also permits partial reliability, stream reset, and interleaving of large user messages; SCTP authentication can be used but adds no benefit when DTLS already protects the traffic.

The RFC states that combining SCTP with DTLS introduces no new security considerations beyond those of the two protocols. SCTP should not process underlying IP addresses because DTLS does not guarantee them. The document requires no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Several SCTP extensions still work with this encapsulation, with a few restrictions on address handling. The RFC identifies no extra security risk from combining SCTP and DTLS.
